idiom_name: hand-written tagged struct (status enum + union payload) plus status-returning functions
implementation_notes: C has no sum type and no exceptions, so the failure contract is a convention carried by the signature: a struct with a status tag plus a union of success and error payloads, built by ok_*/err_* helpers and read only through the tag, since the union holds at most one member at a time. The function-level variant is the status return with an out-parameter for the payload (int rc = parse_port(s, &out)), which forces the caller to check before using the value. errno is a side channel - a thread-local error number meaningful only directly after a failing call - and must not be the primary channel for expected failures; the tagged struct is the honest carrier. Nothing here can be replaced by something smaller in C, so the discipline is design and review, not language enforcement.
pitfalls: Reading the union member that was not last written reinterprets the bytes; every access must be gated by the status tag, and only some compilers diagnose the mistake.
Nothing forces a caller to consume the returned status: a Result in C is a convention, so static analysis and review rules are what keep the failure from being dropped.
errno is meaningful only immediately after a failing call and is not cleared by successful ones; using it as a general failure channel invites stale-value bugs.
